new_statements.quote: 8. Bezüglich der Regeln der Betonung muß darauf geachtet werden, ob ein Wort ein zusammengesetztes oder ein einfaches ist. Bei einfachen zwei- und dreisilbigen Wörtern mit allen oder zwei letzten kurzen Silben ruht die Betonung auf der ersten Silbe. Beispiele: kinji, kneifen; ūjaloñ, breit (Insel); jogajok, Moskito. Ist in dreisilbigen Wörtern die zweite Silbe lang, so erhält diese die Betonung: jeūrur, Unruhe, Aufruhr. Übrigens nimmt die letzte Silbe, falls sie lang und die andern kurz sind, die Betonung an: z. B. jeroān, verschwenden, vergeuden; buīn, sein Geruch.
new_statements.translation: 8. As regards the rules of stress, attention must be paid to whether a word is compound or simple. In simple two- and three-syllable words in which all syllables, or the last two, are short, the stress rests on the first syllable. Examples: kinji 'to pinch'; ūjaloñ 'broad (of an island)'; jogajok 'mosquito'. If in three-syllable words the second syllable is long, it receives the stress: jeūrur 'unrest, uproar'. Moreover, the last syllable takes the stress if it is long and the others are short: e.g. jeroān 'to squander, waste'; buīn 'its smell'. (Vowel-length diacritics on the examples are as read from the page image; the scanned text layer drops some of them.)
new_statements.citation: Erdland, August. 1906. Wörterbuch und Grammatik der Marshall-Sprache nebst ethnographischen Erläuterungen und kurzen Sprachübungen (Archiv für das Studium deutscher Kolonialsprachen, Band IV). Berlin: Georg Reimer.
new_statements.locator: Grammatik, Kapitel I (Lautlehre), §8 'Betonung', p. 198 (PDF page 197 of the archive.org scan bub_gb_-KALAAAAMAAJ; page image verified:)
new_statements.rule_in_words: In simple (underived) words stress falls on the first syllable when the syllables are short; a long syllable (long vowel) attracts the stress, whether it is the second syllable of a trisyllable or the final syllable. Weight-sensitive with initial default. The same section adds morphological conditions: prefixes ka- and ri- do not shift stress (jūdak / kajūdak; belle / ribelle); directional suffixes -dok, -lok, -waj leave stress on the stem (bōge / bōgelok); a directional adverb inserted before such a suffix takes the stress (bōkliñlok, wanlāllak); stress often moves to the following syllable when an object pronoun is suffixed to the verb (āadoñ 'to smell' vs. āadoñe 'smell it'); and a prefixed subject pronoun takes the stress (eiet 'they are few', stem iet).
new_statements.exceptions: Compound vs. simple words treated separately; stem stress retained under ka-/ri- prefixation and -dok/-lok/-waj suffixation; a directional adverb before the suffix is stressed; object-pronoun suffixation often shifts stress rightward; a prefixed subject pronoun (e-, en) takes the stress. No claim that stress is contrastive; no minimal pairs given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for simple words, with statements for derived/inflected verb forms; no distinction between citation and connected-speech forms. Note this is a 1906 missionary description in a pre-phonemic orthography whose vowel-length marking is admitted to be uncertain (p. 196 §4: only long vowels are marked); the modern analyses (Bender 1968/1969, Bender-Capelle-Pagotto 2016) could not be opened and may supersede it, e.g. by treating stress as non-distinctive.
new_statements.identity_note: Erdland 1906 describes Marshallese as a whole; the foreword (p. VI) is dated Jaluit (Ralik chain), 12 June 1904, says he worked on several atolls with older speakers, and notes lexical and vowel divergence between the Radak (Ratak) and Rālik groups without assigning his stress rules to either dialect. Ralik-based description is likely but not stated. Glottolog dialect codes for Ralik/Ratak not verified here.

sources.locator: Grammatik, Kapitel I (Lautlehre), §8 'Betonung', p. 198 (PDF page 197 of the archive.org scan bub_gb_-KALAAAAMAAJ; page image verified:)
sources.note: Grammatik Kap. I §8 (p. 198): stress on the first syllable of simple words with short syllables; a long second syllable in trisyllables, or a long final syllable, takes the stress; prefixes ka-/ri- and suffixes -dok/-lok/-waj do not shift stem stress; directional adverbs, object-pronoun suffixes and subject-pronoun prefixes can shift it. Also p. 195 §3: in vowel sequences the unstressed vowel attaches closely to the stressed one; u is rarely stressed.
